title: Rosalind and the Visitor
premise: Beatrix Winterbourne hosts a late-night radio show in the dying village of Rosalind, where the callers are the recently dead and the frost outside draws patterns no one remembers making. When the melted church bell rings again, Beatrix is pulled into the founders' unfinished ritual — a bargain struck in 1911 to keep winter from taking the village whole, paid for with one memory per villager per year. To survive, Beatrix must complete the ritual before the frost finishes its final pattern, but doing so means surrendering their own memories of everyone they've ever loved. In the end, Beatrix chooses to give up their own name instead, becoming the village's new keeper of the bell — alive, belonging, and remembered by no one.
about_author: Beatrix Eastwick spent a decade as a night-shift radio producer in coastal towns that no longer appear on maps, collecting the stories insomniacs tell when they think no one is listening. They write horror about places that remember people better than people remember themselves.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. On air at 2 a.m., Beatrix takes a call from Mrs. Aldous, who died last Tuesday; the switchboard shows no caller. Beatrix has explained away such things for fifteen years. The emotional beat is weary denial — the practiced calm of someone who has decided survival means not looking too closely.

chapters.title: The Pattern in the Frost
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Frost on Beatrix's window forms the same spiral each morning, growing more intricate. Old Tom Merrick warns them the founders' ledger lists every villager's 'yearly tithe.' Beat: creeping dread as denial begins to crack; Beatrix realizes the patterns are counting down.

chapters.title: What the Bell Was
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix, intercut with 1911 diary entries from founder Edith Rosalind. The bell was melted to forge the ritual's boundary stakes; its ringing was the sound of the bargain being sealed. Beat: vertigo of discovery — the village's history is a mechanism, and Beatrix is inside it.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. The dead callers grow urgent: they are the villagers whose tithes consumed them entirely, erased from memory, existing only on the radio frequency. One caller is someone Beatrix loved and cannot place. Beat: grief without an object — the price of survival made personal.

chapters.title: The Ringing
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. At dusk the melted bell rings across the village; frost erupts in spirals down every street, and Beatrix is pulled through into the ritual's interior — a village beneath the village, preserved in ice. Beat: terror and awe; no more explanations left.

chapters.title: Edith's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV alternating Beatrix and Edith (1911). Inside the frozen under-village, Beatrix finds Edith's final entry: the ritual was left half-finished deliberately, so a successor could choose how it ends. Beat: horrified understanding — the founders built a trap that requires a willing heir.

chapters.title: Tithe
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. The frost offers Beatrix a preview: touch the pattern and lose one memory. They sacrifice small ones first — a childhood dog, a teacher's name — buying time to map the ritual's completion. Beat: complicity; Beatrix starts paying the price they once condemned.

chapters.title: The Final Pattern
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. The frost nears completion; villagers begin forgetting each other mid-conversation, the village unraveling. Beatrix discovers the last stake must be driven by someone who gives up everything — all memory, all identity. Beat: despair sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Rosalind and the Visitor
chapters.summary: POV Beatrix. Climax. In the frozen chapel, Beatrix completes the ritual, offering not their memories but their name — reframing the bargain so the village keeps its people and the keeper keeps nothing. The bell rings once, warmly. Beat: self-annihilation as an act of love and belonging.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV unnamed radio host. A new voice runs the late-night show; no one in Rosalind recalls who held the job before, only that someone always has. The frost lies still. On the switchboard, one light glows: a caller with no name, saying thank you. Beat: bittersweet resolution — survival achieved, memory the cost, belonging found in erasure.
